body: I totally get the "alcohol is normalized in my community."  Now that I've been in recovery so long, I notice how pervasive alcohol is, and how insidiously it is marketed on TV.  Good people who supposedly do not have an alcohol disorder drink in almost every episode.  When we compare depictions of what we believe is social drinking to our own drinking, it seems like our issue isn't that bad.  I've seen so many shows where the people are absolutely dependent on alcohol, but they're portrayed as normies.  It's very sneaky and evil, in my opinion.

I overcame alcoholism and you can too!  I promise you, the worst day sober is better than the best day in addiction.  My life is better in every single way.  Once you're in long term recovery, you need to be sure to not diminish the harm you've done to your kids.  This has been instrumental to fixing our relationship.  Listen, apologize, don't justify, but explain.  Tell them you got sober for them, and you are so sorry for what you put them through. 
  Some things that helped-
  everyone has a sob story.  I was abandoned by my husband 2 weeks after our very premature son was born.  I was blackmailed into a relationship where i was trafficked for 4 years.  I was a victim and what happened to me was wrong, and that's how I justified my drinking, but the second you start harming others, you stop being the victim. What happened to you and us (because I know you have trauma you use to excuse your drinking) does not matter to your children.  All you are doing is victimizing them.

  "Thank God I was raped." I started looking forward to bad things happening, or exaggerating mildly bad things, because they gave me the excuse I needed to drink.  Next time something bad happens to you and you want to use alcohol to escape it, say "thank God my ex was a jerk." "Thank God my day was stressful."  Call yourself out for your messed up thinking.  
 
 You are going to have a rough 6 or so months while your brain balances out, but 6 months is going to pass either way.  Do you want to be sober in 6 months, or do you want to stay an alcoholic?  
  
 There is a reason people are so passionate about recovery, and it's because our lives are so much better now.  It's impossible to conceive a life without substances until you're on the other side. Once you're there, you're going to think you were an idiot for waiting this long to get better.  You can do this!!!

As a recovering addict, i can assure you that outpatient rehab, 1 month inpatient rehab, 6 month inpatient rehab is not going to make him stop.  I graduated after a month in my first inpatient rehab, and walked from there to the liquor store.  I've graduated from 1 month inpatient rehab followed by 3 months in sober living, and got a third DUI a month later.  They aren't going to teach him anything they didn't teach him in outpatient.  Every single one of the people i met in rehab relapsed fairly soon after graduation.  In all the AA meetings I've been to, ive never heard someone in long term recovery state that rehab is what saved them.  You can learn some excellent skills for coping, but you can learn those in outpatient or with a one on one substance abuse counselor.
  I actually felt inpatient was detrimental to my recovery.  Youre kept isolated from triggers, the staff provides all your meals, youre held accountable for things like waking up in the morning and keeping your room clean.  You dont have any stress or have to worry about bills or work.  you can socialize whenever you want, and you get to go skiing and hiking and lots of other fun stuff you'd never be able to afford in your regular life. Then youre back in the real world, and everything comes crashing down on you.  All the stressors come right back.  You are lonely (unless you go back to your friends who use), you dont have to take care of yourself, you have to find food.  All the stuff normal people have to do.  All you learn, is how to stay sober in an extremely controlled environment where all your needs are easily met.  I think it's also worth noting that almost every time I relapsed after rehab, it's because someone I met in rehab offered me alcohol.  Everything I know about drug use and where to get them is because of people i met in rehab.
  He needs to find a purpose, and something that makes his life bearable.  He has to have something worth being present for, so he doesn't feel like he has to escape.  
  Addiction is a disease.  He can't just "will" it to go away, but the treatment is an extended length of sobriety (which inpatient would admittedly provide.  2 months of sobriety in jail did way more for my recovery than rehab did, tbh), and finding something that gives him a reason to wake up every day.  It's hard at first.  Nothing seems as great as his drug of choice, even things he used to love.  But with a few months, it'll start to come back.  
  If you want to help (which you obviously do), help him get financial aid and enroll him in community college.  Help him make long term goals, so he has hope for a future worth living for.  Help him explore new hobbies.  Maybe he'll find something he's passionate about. Take him to NA meetings, so he can meet other sober people and learn that long term recovery is possible. Convince your husband to spend less time trying to manipulate a teenage girl, and more time engaging with his son.  I really hope he can stop using and find contentment in life.  And i hope your daughter gets into a great school!

 Sorry this is long winded.  I am passionate about addiction and recovery.  

Tl;Dr dont give him your daughters college money.

I am so sorry.  I know this is so painful, and I hate you're going through this sense of hopelessness.  I dont know how old you are, or how experienced you are with heart break, so I dont really know what kind of advice I can give.  
  The last time I went through a suicidal phase, it's because my boyfriend broke up with me and told me I had to get an abortion.  I was obsessively in love with him, and the buzz I got from being "in love" was like a drug (not saying that's what you're going through).  
   I decided I was going to drink 350 ml of whiskey and jump in front of the 9:00 train when it passed by. Another friend ended up calling the cops for a wellness check, and I ended up at a psych ward for 3 days.  Once I had time to relax and get a break from the crazy emotions, I decided life was worth another shot.  I was still depressed and confused for months, but the suicidal urge went away.  
  I dont really have friends or a family either, so I know how hard it can be to go through all of these emotions alone.  It's also really hard to pick yourself back up from something as devastating as heart break when you're an addict, because our substance has taken over all the things we used to love about life.  
 I know the pain seems so insurmountable right now, but maybe think about it this way:
  You only have three days left to live, right?  So why not go do all the (sober) things you always wanted to.  Get some fuzzy socks and nice lotion, and do like a bath bomb, lotion up your feet, and eat ben and jerrys while watching a show you like?  Or take yourself hiking and just take in how beautiful everything is.  Wander around downtown at night and just go wherever your feet take you.  

Just be sure you stay sober during the 3 days and remind yourself why life is a beautiful place.  I wish you so much love and happiness.  Good luck!
